extracted.intended_audience: novice and intermediate TeX users / typists learning to typeset documents with plain TeX
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance from a TeX manual on distinguishing primitives vs macros, choosing and loading fonts, using grouping and local/global definitions, and basic procedures for running TeX and preparing documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish primitives from defined control sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ways to tell a primitive from a higher-level defined control sequence: the manual's index marks primitives with an asterisk, and you can display the meaning of a control sequence while running TeX by typing \show\cs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: :\show\input) yields :> \input=\input.) because \input is primitive; :\show\thinspace) yields \thinspace=macro: ->\kern .16667em., showing \thinspace is a macro. Results of \show appear on the terminal and in the log file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with plain TeX and adapt gradually
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX is a set of about 600 basic control sequences defined in Appendix B (together with ~300 primitives) and is usually present when TeX starts; it is a reasonable foundation for learning and building formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can design radically different formats by changing a dozen or so definitions; the best way to learn is to start with plain TeX and change its definitions little by little. If you create formats others will use, write a supplement explaining your style rules. Appendix E shows example formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font-changing control sequences in plain TeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides control sequences to switch typefaces: \rm (roman), \sl (slanted roman), \it (italic), \tt (typewriter), \bf (bold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the beginning of a run you get \rm unless specified otherwise. Prefer grouping (braces) to localize font changes rather than repeatedly typing \rm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer grouping (braces) to confine local font/definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use { and } to group text so font changes or definitions inside the group do not affect text outside; grouping implements local (block-structured) changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to make only a phrase bold or slanted use {\bf bold} or {\sl emphasize}. Grouping also stops TeX from absorbing optional spaces after control sequences when used like {\TeX}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empty group or braces to prevent space gobbling after control sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent TeX from swallowing an optional space after a control sequence, either enclose the control sequence in braces ({\TeX}) or follow it by an empty group (\TeX{}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is handy when using a text editor or when replacing words by control sequences so the next normal character isn't treated as part of the control sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic correction (\/ ) when switching from slanted/italic to unslanted text
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX provides \/, the italic correction, which adjusts spacing when switching from slanted or italic back to roman or bold; the correction varies by preceding letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb: use \/ just before switching from slanted or italic to roman or bold, unless the next character is a period or comma. Example: {\it italics\/} for {\it emphasis}. When an italicized word occurs before a semicolon the author recommends typing '{\it word\/};'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation convention with italicized words is changing
rubrics_metrics.description: Old style says punctuation after a word should be in the same font as that word, but this convention is evolving because italic punctuation often looks wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an italicized word occurs just before punctuation (like a semicolon), prefer to keep punctuation in roman by using the italic correction and bracing, e.g., '{\it word\/};'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null font availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The primitive control sequence \nullfont represents a font that has no characters; it is always present in case no fonts have been specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font naming and size conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each font is associated with a control sequence name (e.g., \tenrm for 10-point roman, \ninerm for 9-point). \rm may be set up to mean 'roman in current size' while \tenrm means 'roman in 10-point size'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formats can redefine abbreviations like \rm and \sl depending on current document size (e.g., \tenpoint, \ninepoint). In plain TeX \rm usually gets you \tenrm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loading fonts into TeX memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \font\cs=(external font name) to load information about a particular font into TeX's memory; afterwards \cs selects that font for typesetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \font\ninerm=cmr9. Plain TeX provides a limited initial set (about sixteen fonts); you can use \font to access fonts in your system's library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale fonts carefully; prefer slight scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: A font can be magnified or shrunk (e.g., \font\magnifiedfiverm=cmr5 at 10pt or scaled 2000), but well-designed fonts are drawn differently at different design sizes, so scaling affects appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is usually best to scale fonts only slightly relative to their design size unless the final product will be photographically reduced or you want an unusual effect. Check that your typesetter supports the requested size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TeX's magstep scaling for system-wide consistent magnifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides \magstep0..\magstep5 and \magstephalf abbreviations for common geometric magnifications (1000, 1200, 1440, ...); use scaled \magstep values to bring fonts in at standard magnifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \font\bigtenrm=cmr10 scaled\magstep2. Also be aware that an overall \magnification interacts additively with font scaling (e.g., loading at \magstep1 plus \magnification=\magstep2 gives printed \magstep3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive font switching; roman for sustained reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Special fonts (bold, slanted, italic) are effective for emphasis but tiring for sustained reading; roman type should account for most of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't get carried away with font switching unless there is good reason; prefer grouping to manage occasional emphasis rather than global font changes everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs global definitions; use \global when persistence is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and parameter changes made inside a group are local and are restored when the group ends; prefixing \global to a definition makes it persist beyond the current group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: output routines are protected by groups; to increase a page number inside an output routine use \global\advance\count0 by 1 so the change remains after the group ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \begingroup and \endgroup for grouping across control sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The primitives \begingroup and \endgroup provide a way to begin and end groups within different control sequences, helping to obtain block structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX's executed text (after expansion) must have properly nested groups that don't overlap; malformed nesting like '{ \begingroup } \endgroup' is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish control sequences that act on the next token vs those that change state
rubrics_metrics.description: Some control sequences (e.g., \centerline) apply only to the very next thing that follows and therefore require braces to group multi-word arguments; others (e.g., \it) change the current font and affect everything that follows unless confined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To center a multi-word phrase use \centerline{...}. To limit the scope of \it use braces, e.g., {\it text\/}.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX workflow: starting TeX, \relax, and input files
rubrics_metrics.description: To start TeX you typically invoke the program (e.g., 'tex' or 'run tex'), TeX prompts with '**' asking for an input file name; typing \relax and return is a simple way to begin an interactive run without input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the first character you type at '**' is not a backslash, TeX inserts '\input' automatically, so you can usually run 'tex filename' or simply type the filename at the '**' prompt. Use \end to finish a run; TeX writes a .dvi file (e.g., texput.dvi) as device-independent output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ampersand (&) at initial prompt to load precomputed format
rubrics_metrics.description: If the first character after '**' is an ampersand (&) TeX will replace its memory with a precomputed format file before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '&plain story' or '&plain \input story' loads the plain format first, which is useful if your TeX invocation doesn't have plain preloaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX handles paragraph line breaking and hyphenation automatically
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't need to manually break lines in paragraphs; TeX reads paragraphs (terminated by a blank line) and determines line breaks and hyphenation to equalize spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscript files can have long or short lines; TeX will reformat. Vertical skips and constructs like \vskip are not part of paragraphs and affect paragraph boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties (~) to prevent line breaks between words
rubrics_metrics.description: Ties (the '~' character) act like normal spaces but prevent TeX from breaking a line at that point; they are useful within names and places where a break should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example uses shown in the story.tex sample: use ties within names to keep components on the same line; further discussion appears in Chapter 14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check device/font support when requesting arbitrary sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX accepts any positive font size less than 2048 points, but the final output will be incorrect unless the scaled font is actually available on your output device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using 'at' or large scaling factors, verify that your typesetter/printer supports the requested size.
